data.text/markdown:
What does one answer cost an AI agent through a public data MCP server?

Public data publishers are putting MCP servers in front of their data so AI agents can query it. Each answer an agent gets costs its user tokens, tool calls, time and money. We expect that cost to differ by an order of magnitude between servers, and to depend less on the data than on how the tools are designed: how many calls it takes to get valid filter codes, how much each result returns, and whether results carry their own citation. We ask about 20 questions with known answers through each of three public servers, with the same client and model, and count what every answer costs and whether it is right:
  • HIFLD Next (/mcp): US infrastructure, 400+ datasets, run by Public Environmental Data Partners. We built it.
  • mcp.mospi.gov.in: Indian official statistics from India's Ministry of Statistics (MoSPI).
  • Education Data Portal: US schools, districts and colleges, from the Urban Institute.
Then we make one design change to HIFLD Next, on our side of the wire, and rerun it.

1. What each server sends before the first question

An MCP client sends every tool's name, description and input schema to the model on every request, plus the server's instructions if it has any. That is a fixed cost per step, paid before any data comes back. Here is what each server ships, read straight from the servers.

data.text/markdown:
2. The questions

One set per server, written the way that server's users would ask, each with one answer we looked up ourselves from the publisher's own API (the how_found column has the exact call, so anyone can check the key). Numbers carry a tolerance for honest rounding; names carry the strings we accept. The questions differ by server because the data does; section 7 comes back to what that does to the comparison.

data.text/markdown:
3. One client, one model

A Pydantic AI agent connects to each server as shipped: every tool it lists, and its instructions if it sends any (Urban's server does; the other two don't). The model is Claude Haiku 5.5 on OpenRouter, which reports the dollar cost of each request. The agent must return a typed answer: a sentence, the number if there is one, and the source a reader could use to check it. Our instructions say nothing about any server, so the only guidance it gets is what the server itself provides. A run stops at 25 model requests or 5 minutes.

4. Run every question through its server

Four questions run at a time per server. Each run's full transcript is saved to outputs/transcripts/ and its usage to outputs/runs_*.jsonl, so the scoring below can be rerun or changed without paying for model calls (RESCORE=1 ./run.sh).

5. Score every answer

Correct: a number within the key's tolerance, or a name containing one of the strings the key accepts. Checkable source: the answer gives a URL on the publisher's own domain that opens (HTTP status below 400) and is more than the home page. A named dataset with no link doesn't count, because a reader can't click it; we report it separately as has_citation. Failed runs count as wrong and their cost counts.

data.text/markdown:
Where the tokens go

The first request of a run holds only the instructions, the tool definitions and the question, so its input tokens are the fixed price of one step on that server. Every later step resends that, plus everything the tools have returned so far. So two things drive tokens: the fixed price times the number of steps, and how much data the tools return. fixed_share is the fixed price times the steps, as a share of all input tokens.

data.text/markdown:
7. One design change on HIFLD Next

HIFLD Next's MCP server ships map-widget tools for clients that can show an MCP Apps map. Their definitions are long, and a client sends them to the model on every step whether or not it can draw a map. The change: list those tools only to clients that render MCP Apps UI. A client declares that when it connects, so the server can do this itself; here we do it on our side, by dropping every tool the server marks with a UI resource, and leave the production server alone. Everything else is the same: same questions, model and instructions.

data.text/markdown:
8. Does it hold?

On cost, it fails. Cost per correct answer runs from ||(0.0068** to **||)0.0155, a 2.3x spread, not an order of magnitude. All three servers answer for about a cent. On what drives the cost, it holds. The most expensive server is not the one with the most data or the biggest results. HIFLD Next costs most because of what it sends before any data: its tool definitions are 71% of its input tokens. Dropping the map tools from its list changed its cost per answer by -39% (fixed tokens per step 17,023 → 6,886) with no loss of accuracy (100% → 100% correct), and the spread falls to 1.4x. The difference that is large is the citation. Urban's results carry a link in every result and 100% of its answers pass one on; HIFLD Next's carry file URLs and 98% do. MoSPI's results carry no link, so 0% of its answers cite one taken from a tool result. Its answers were right, but a reader has no link to check them by.

9. What this doesn't show

  • The questions were easy for this model. Almost every answer was right, so cost per correct answer is nearly cost per answer. Harder questions (the judgment calls Urban's own study found agents get wrong) would separate the servers on accuracy, which this set can't.
  • Questions differ by server, because the data does. A MoSPI question needs a dataset, an indicator and filter codes; an HIFLD question often needs SQL over a file. We pinned every question to one answer, but not to equal difficulty.
  • One client and one model. Pydantic AI sends every listed tool on every step and the server's instructions verbatim. A client that defers tool definitions until needed would erase most of HIFLD Next's fixed cost, and another model may take more or fewer steps.
  • Prices date. Haiku 5.5 costs $0.10 per million input tokens on OpenRouter; tokens and steps are the numbers that will hold up.
  • The link check is mechanical. MoSPI's API host refuses modern TLS clients (it needs legacy renegotiation), so links an agent built to it fail our check even when they may open in some browsers. link_from_tools doesn't depend on that: it asks only whether the link came from a tool result.
  • We built HIFLD Next, so read its numbers knowing that. Its server costs most of the three as shipped.
